title: Distinct Echo Substrings
description: Brute force to optimized: comparing every half directly versus a precomputed rolling hash for O(1) half comparisons.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given a string text, return the number of distinct substrings that are an "echo" substring, meaning the substring can be written as some string A concatenated with itself (A plus A), such as "abcabc" being "abc" plus "abc".

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a string text, return the number of distinct substrings that are an "echo" substring, meaning the substring can be written as some string A concatenated with itself (A plus A), such as "abcabc" being "abc" plus "abc".

blocks.text: Like scanning a long string of letters for every distinct stretch where a shorter phrase is immediately followed by an exact repeat of itself, the way "hoho" is just "ho" said twice in a row.

No substring of this text can be split into two identical halves, so the answer is 0.
5. How Should We Think?
It helps to ask whether comparing two halves of a substring really requires walking through every character each time.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force checks every possible even length substring, splits it exactly in half, and compares the two halves character by character, which costs up to O(n) per candidate on top of O(n squared) candidates.

Observation 2: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String already showed that a rolling hash, precomputed once over the whole string, lets any substring's hash be retrieved in O(1), the same tool used there to compare a sliding window against a fixed pattern.

Observation 3: That same precomputed hash can just as easily compare two arbitrary substrings against each other, here, the two halves of a candidate echo, turning each half-versus-half comparison into a single O(1) hash comparison instead of a full character scan.

Observation 4: Exactly as with substring search, a hash match is only a candidate, so a direct character comparison is still required afterward to rule out a coincidental collision, confirmed by tracing text equal to "abcabcabc", where the candidate at indices 0 to 5 has its two halves' hashes match instantly, gets verified directly, and correctly contributes to the final count of 3 distinct echo substrings.

Recognizing that a rolling hash can compare any two substrings against each other, not just a sliding window against a fixed pattern, is what turns an O(n) per-candidate character comparison into an O(1) hash lookup.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every possible even length substring directly, split it exactly in half, and compare the two halves character by character, keeping every distinct match in a set.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every starting position and every even length, extract the substring.
Split it into a first half and a second half of equal length.
Compare the two halves character by character, and if they match, add the whole substring to a set of found echoes.

codes.python:
def distinct_echo_substrings(text):
    n = len(text)
    found = set()
    for start in range(n):
        for length in range(2, n - start + 1, 2):                   # only even lengths can possibly split evenly
            half = length // 2
            first_half = text[start:start + half]
            second_half = text[start + half:start + length]
            if first_half == second_half:                              # direct character by character comparison
                found.add(text[start:start + length])
    return len(found)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    text = "abcabcabc"
    print(distinct_echo_substrings(text))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Only even lengths are ever tried, since an odd length substring can never split into two equal, non empty halves.
Each candidate's two halves are compared directly for equality, which correctly identifies genuine echo substrings.
A set is used to store found echoes, since it naturally collapses duplicate values found at different starting positions.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every possible even length substring is directly split and compared, so every genuine echo substring is correctly found, and the set naturally handles distinctness.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n cubed), for O(n squared) candidate substrings, each requiring up to O(n) to compare its two halves.
Space: O(n squared), for the set of found substrings in the worst case.

Limitation: comparing the two halves character by character every single time is expensive, when a single precomputed hash of the whole string could compare any two substrings of the same length in constant time instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: comparing two halves character by character for every one of the O(n squared) candidate substrings adds an extra O(n) factor that a lookup could avoid entirely.

What a precomputed rolling hash fixes: once built, the hash of any substring can be retrieved in O(1), so comparing two substrings becomes a single number comparison instead of a full character scan.

What still has to be checked after a hash match: a direct character comparison, since a hash match alone does not rule out a coincidental collision between two different substrings.

The core idea: precompute the hash array once, compare each candidate's two halves in O(1), and verify directly only when the hashes actually match.

Precompute a rolling polynomial hash prefix array for the entire text once, which allows the hash of any substring to be computed in constant time from the prefix hashes. Then, for every candidate even length substring, compare the hash of its first half against the hash of its second half in O(1), only falling back to a direct character comparison on a hash match, to guard against a rare hash collision.
9. Optimized Solution
A precomputed prefix hash array turns each half comparison into a constant time hash comparison.
Dry run for text = "abcabcabc", checking the substring at indices 0 to 5 ("abcabc")

blocks.caption: Optimized: a precomputed prefix hash array turns each half comparison into O(1)

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because the precomputed prefix hash array lets the hash of any substring be derived algebraically in O(1) from just two prefix values and a power of the base, so comparing two substrings' hashes correctly identifies almost every genuine match, and the follow up direct comparison guarantees correctness even in the rare case of a coincidental hash collision.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) average, since each of the O(n squared) candidate substrings is now checked in O(1) with only rare direct verifications.
Space: O(n), for the prefix hash and power arrays.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Precomputed rolling hashes are the standard way to turn many repeated substring comparisons into constant time lookups, at the cost of needing an occasional direct verification to guard against the small chance of a hash collision.
Common Mistakes

items: Skipping the direct character verification after a hash match, risking a false positive from a hash collision being counted as a real echo substring.
Forgetting that only even lengths can ever split into two equal, non empty halves, and wasting time checking odd lengths.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Mention that achieving better than O(n squared) for this exact problem typically requires more advanced structures like a suffix automaton, which is well beyond what is expected in a standard interview setting for this problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid comparing every half character by character", think: a precomputed rolling hash, comparing halves in O(1).
If the interviewer says "what if two different substrings hash the same", think: always verify a hash match with a direct character comparison before counting it.
If the interviewer says "can you do better than O(n squared)", think: mention a suffix automaton or similar advanced structure exists, but it is well beyond what this problem typically expects.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why must a hash match always be confirmed with a direct character comparison?
Why can only even length substrings ever be echo substrings?
How would you adapt this approach to count substrings that are three repeated copies of some string A, instead of exactly two?
How would you return the actual echo substrings found, not just their count?
How would this approach change if the string could be extremely long, making even O(n squared) too slow?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String, whose rolling hash technique is reused here directly, just comparing two substrings to each other instead of a window to a fixed pattern.
Repeated Substring Pattern and Longest Happy Prefix, other problems that reason about a string's self similarity, though those use the KMP prefix-suffix array rather than a rolling hash.
Any problem requiring many pairwise substring comparisons, where precomputing a rolling hash once turns each comparison into an O(1) lookup instead of a fresh character scan.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n cubed) time, O(n squared) space. Optimized (rolling hash): O(n squared) average time, O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a precomputed rolling hash over the whole string, turning every half-versus-half comparison into an O(1) lookup.

Core Idea: the same rolling hash technique used for substring search can compare any two substrings against each other, turning an O(n) half comparison into an O(1) hash comparison, with a direct verification only when hashes actually match.
Time: O(n cubed) for the brute force, O(n squared) average for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a rolling hash is a general purpose tool for comparing any two substrings quickly, not limited to sliding a window against one fixed pattern.

Interview Difficulty: the rolling hash mechanics themselves are the hard part to get exactly right; forgetting the verification step is the most common way this approach silently produces wrong answers.
One line memory trick: hash each half in O(1), compare the numbers, and verify directly before counting a match.
